title: DAPR Data Management and Visualization Pipeline
text:
1 Introduction & Setup
This guidebook is intended to teach the fundamentals of data management and data visualization using R and Python. The guide was created and is maintained by the Data Science and Analytics for Precision Rehabilitation (DAPR) Center, funded by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (P50-HD118603). The original code was written by KRL in R with a rough draft in Python, Google Gemini 3.6 was then used to troubleshoot Python code and bundle all scripts as a Quarto Notebook. Accuracy of all final code was confirmed and didactic comments added by KRL.
The guide walks through basic steps of data management - such importing data, merging files, and calculating variables - to data visualizaton for different purposed - from basic figures for quality assurance, to static figures to publication, to interactive and animated figures.
As our example data set, we will use the openly available Balance Data Set (BDS) from Santos & Duarte (2016). In this study, N=163 younger and older adults stood on a force plate under two different visual conditions (eyes open versus eyes closed) and on two different surfaces (a firm surface and a foam surface) for three trials in each condition (making 12 total trials per participant). Each trial lasted 60 seconds and force plate data were sampled at 100 Hz. This gives us an incredibly rich data set for learning how to manage and visualize data in the rehabilitation sciences (e.g., 163 people x 12 trials x 60 secs x 100 samples per second x 3 different force plate axes).

title: Interactive Data Visualization
text:
1 Introduction
While static graphics are ideal for publication, interactive visualizations are essential for data exploration and quality assurance (QA). Interactive tooltips allow researchers to inspect individual outliers, verify data flags, and examine subject metadata without cluttering the plot canvas.
In this module, we demonstrate how to build interactive figures: * In R, we use ggiraph, which extends ggplot2 syntax by converting standard geoms into interactive HTML elements. * In Python, we use plotly (plotly.express and plotly.graph_objects), which creates web-ready JavaScript widgets from pandas DataFrames.



2 Interactive Postural Sway Across Conditions
In this first example, we make our multi-condition postural sway trajectories interactive. Hovering over any point displays subject metadata (Subject ID, Age, Gender, and Total Path Length), and hovering over an individual point highlights the subject’s entire trajectory across conditions.

R (ggplot2 & ggiraph)Python (plotly)




Show Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggiraph)

# 1. Load Summary Data & Aggregate to Subject Averages
DATA <- readRDS("./data/BDS/output/BDS_trial_summary.rds") %>% 
  mutate(
    Subject  = factor(Subject),
    AgeGroup = fct_relevel(AgeGroup, "Young", "Old")
  )

AVE_DATA <- DATA %>% 
  select(-Trial) %>%
  group_by(Subject, Vision, Surface) %>%
  summarise(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    across(!where(is.numeric), dplyr::first),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Condition = factor(paste0(Surface, ":", Vision),
                       levels = c("Firm:Open", "Firm:Closed", "Foam:Open", "Foam:Closed"))
  )

# 2. Build Tooltip Text
AVE_DATA <- AVE_DATA %>%
  mutate(tooltip_text = paste0(
    "<b>Subject ID:</b> ", Subject, "<br>",
    "<b>Age:</b> ", round(Age, 1), " years<br>",
    "<b>Gender:</b> ", Gender, "<br>",
    "<b>Sway (Path Length):</b> ", round(PathLength_Total, 1), " cm"
  ))

# 3. Define Colorblind Palette
cbPalette <- c("#1E6654", "#CC5500", "#954535", "#5B7C99")

# 4. Create Interactive ggplot
p_sway <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, 
                 aes(x = Condition, y = PathLength_Total,
                     tooltip = tooltip_text, data_id = Subject)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Subject),
            color = "gray75", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_point_interactive(aes(shape = Condition, col = Condition, group = Subject), 
                         size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7, position = position_dodge(width = 0.2),
                         hover_nearest = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ AgeGroup) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Postural Sway: Between- and Within-Subject Effects",
    subtitle = "Hover points to inspect subject metadata; lines connect individual trajectories",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total Path Length (cm)",
    shape = "Condition", col = "Condition", fill = "Condition"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, face = "italic", color = "gray30"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

# 5. Render Interactive girafe Widget
girafe(
  ggobj = p_sway,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill:red;stroke:black;r:5pt;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;"),
    opts_tooltip(css = "background-color:black;color:white;padding:8px;border-radius:4px;font-family:sans-serif;")
  )
)










Show Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# 1. Load Summary Data & Aggregate to Subject Averages
DATA = pd.read_csv("./data/BDS/output/BDS_trial_summary.csv")
DATA["AgeGroup"] = pd.Categorical(DATA["AgeGroup"], categories=["Young", "Old"], ordered=True)

meta_cols = ["Subject", "Vision", "Surface", "AgeGroup", "Gender"]
AVE_DATA = DATA.groupby(meta_cols, as_index=False, observed=True).mean(numeric_only=True)
AVE_DATA["Condition"] = AVE_DATA["Surface"].astype(str) + ":" + AVE_DATA["Vision"].astype(str)

cond_order = ["Firm:Open", "Firm:Closed", "Foam:Open", "Foam:Closed"]
cbPalette = ["#1E6654", "#CC5500", "#954535", "#5B7C99"]
cond_colors = {cond: cbPalette[i] for i, cond in enumerate(cond_order)}

# 2. Build Base Scatter Plot
fig1 = px.scatter(
    AVE_DATA,
    x="Condition",
    y="PathLength_Total",
    color="Condition",
    symbol="Condition",
    facet_col="AgeGroup",
    category_orders={"AgeGroup": ["Young", "Old"], "Condition": cond_order},
    color_discrete_map=cond_colors,
    custom_data=["Subject", "Age", "Gender", "PathLength_Total"],
    labels={"PathLength_Total": "Total Path Length (cm)", "Condition": "Condition"},
    title="<b>Postural Sway: Between- and Within-Subject Effects</b><br><sup>Hover points to inspect subject metadata; lines connect individual trajectories</sup>"
)

# 3. Add Within-Subject Trajectory Lines Across Subplots
for i, age_grp in enumerate(["Young", "Old"], start=1):
    sub_df = AVE_DATA[AVE_DATA["AgeGroup"] == age_grp]
    for sub_id, grp in sub_df.groupby("Subject"):
        grp_sorted = grp.set_index("Condition").reindex(cond_order).dropna().reset_index()
        fig1.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=grp_sorted["Condition"],
                y=grp_sorted["PathLength_Total"],
                mode="lines",
                line=dict(color="rgba(180, 180, 180, 0.5)", width=1),
                showlegend=False,
                hoverinfo="skip"
            ),
            row=1, col=i
        )

# Move trajectory lines behind scatter points
n_conditions = len(cond_order)
fig1.data = tuple(list(fig1.data[n_conditions:]) + list(fig1.data[:n_conditions]))

# 4. Format Custom Hover Tooltip & Layout
fig1.update_traces(
    selector=dict(mode="markers"),
    marker=dict(size=8, opacity=0.8),
    hovertemplate=(
        "<b>Subject ID:</b> %{customdata[0]}<br>"
        "<b>Age:</b> %{customdata[1]:.1f} years<br>"
        "<b>Gender:</b> %{customdata[2]}<br>"
        "<b>Sway (Path Length):</b> %{customdata[3]:.1f} cm<extra></extra>"
    )
)

fig1.update_layout(
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.2, x=0.5, xanchor="center"),
    height=500
)

3 Interactive Quality Assurance (Force Plate Calibration & Unweighting)
In this second example, we evaluate force plate calibration and screen for potential artifacts (such as a participant stepping off or unweighting the platform).
Under static gravity, vertical force \(F_z\) should approximate body weight in Newtons:
\[F_z \approx \text{Mass (kg)} \times 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2\]
Hovering over flagged data points instantly reveals trial parameters, recorded body weight, and minimum vs. median \(F_z\) values.

R (ggplot2 & ggiraph)Python (plotly)




Show Code
# 1. Prepare Interactive Tooltips with Detailed QA Information
QA_data <- DATA %>%
  mutate(
    QA_tooltip = paste0(
      "<b>Subject:</b> ", Subject, " (", AgeGroup, ", ", Gender, ")<br>",
      "<b>Trial:</b> ", Trial, "<br>",
      "<b>Condition:</b> ", Surface, " - ", Vision, "<br>",
      "<b>Recorded Weight:</b> ", Weight, " kg<br>",
      "<b>Median Fz:</b> ", round(Fz_median, 1), " N<br>",
      "<b>Min Fz:</b> ", round(Fz_min, 1), " N<br>",
      "<b>Duration:</b> ", duration_s, "s (", n_samples, " samples)<br>",
      "<b>Flagged?:</b> ", ifelse(flag_any, "⚠️ YES", "✅ No")
    )
  )

# 2. Build Interactive Scatter Plot
qa_plot <- ggplot(QA_data, aes(x = Weight, y = Fz_median, tooltip = QA_tooltip, data_id = Trial)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 9.81, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point_interactive(aes(color = flag_any), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#1E6654", "TRUE" = "#CC5500"), 
    labels = c("Clean", "Flagged"), 
    name = "Data Status"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ AgeGroup) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "QA: Force Plate Calibration & Unweighting Verification",
    subtitle = "Dashed line represents theoretical gravity (Fz = Mass * 9.81). Hover points to inspect anomalies.",
    x = "Recorded Weight (kg)",
    y = "Median Vertical Force Fz (N)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, face = "italic", color = "gray30"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

# 3. Render girafe Widget
girafe(
  ggobj = qa_plot,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill:red;stroke:black;r:6pt;"),
    opts_tooltip(css = "background-color:black;color:white;padding:10px;border-radius:5px;font-family:sans-serif;")
  )
)

title: Data Import & Quality Assurance
text:
1 Import and Merge Data
As mentioned above, we will be using the data from this study by Santos & Duarte (2016): https://peerj.com/articles/2648/ . If you want to run the code below on your local machine, please follow the links in their PeerJ article to download their data from FigShare. Alternatively, if you just want to follow along with the code, you can see all of the code, outputs, and figures below without having to download any data.
If you do download the data, please save it in this structure:
YOUR_FOLDER_HERE/               # Name of the project folder on your local computer
└── data/                       # data subfolder
    └── BDS/                
        ├── trials/              # These are the individual trials data files downloaded from Figshare
            └── BDS00001.csv         # 60s of stabilometer data for trial 1
            └── ...
            └── BDS01956.csv         # 60s of stabilometer data for trial 1956
        └── output/             # This is where we will store outputs generated by the code
        └── BDSinfo.csv         # This is the demographic datafile from FigShare. This file maps trials to subjects.
        # Note that on figshare, the BDSinfo.csv is in the same folder as the individual trial data
        # we move it out of that folder to make some of our automated steps easier.

library(reticulate)
use_condaenv("r-reticulate", required = TRUE)

library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)
library(arrow)

# 1. Read metadata
info_path <- "./data/BDS/BDSinfo.txt"
info_raw  <- read_tsv(info_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

info <- info_raw %>%
  select(Trial, Subject, Vision, Surface, Age, AgeGroup, Gender, Height, Weight, BMI) %>%
  mutate(
    Subject  = as.integer(Subject),
    Vision   = factor(Vision, levels = c("Open", "Closed")),
    Surface  = factor(Surface, levels = c("Firm", "Foam")),
    AgeGroup = factor(AgeGroup),
    Gender   = factor(Gender)
  )

# 2. Batch-read raw trial files
trial_files <- list.files("./data/BDS/trials", pattern = "^BDS\\d+\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE)
trial_ids   <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(trial_files))

read_one_trial <- function(path, trial_id) {
  fread(path, header = TRUE, sep = "\t", showProgress = FALSE) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    rename_with(~ str_trim(str_remove(.x, "\\[.*\\]"))) %>%
    mutate(Trial = trial_id, .before = 1)
}

trial_list <- map2(trial_files, trial_ids, read_one_trial)
all_trials <- bind_rows(trial_list)

# 3. Merge & Save
master <- all_trials %>%
  left_join(info, by = "Trial") %>%
  relocate(Trial, Subject, Vision, Surface, Age, AgeGroup, Gender, Height, Weight, BMI, .before = Time)

dir.create("./data/BDS/output", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
arrow::write_parquet(master, "./data/BDS/output/BDS_master.parquet")
glimpse(master)

2 Quality Assurance & Feature Extraction
From raw Center of Pressure (COP) time-series data \((COP_x, COP_y)\), we extract key biomechanical features:

Path Lengths: Sum of absolute step distances across axes: \[\text{PathLength}_{\text{AP}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} |COP_{y, n+1} - COP_{y, n}|\] \[\text{PathLength}_{\text{Total}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} \sqrt{(COP_{x, n+1} - COP_{x, n})^2 + (COP_{y, n+1} - COP_{y, n})^2}\]
95% Confidence Ellipse Area & Boundary: \[\text{Area}_{95} = 2 \pi F_{0.95, 2, N-2} \sqrt{\lambda_1 \lambda_2}\] where \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) are eigenvalues of the \((COP_x, COP_y)\) covariance matrix.


R (tidyverse & patchwork)Python (numpy, scipy & matplotlib)




Show Code
library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)
library(patchwork)

master <- arrow::read_parquet("./data/BDS/output/BDS_master.parquet")

# 1. Feature Extraction & Ellipse Math
compute_path_metrics <- function(x, y, duration_s) {
  dx <- diff(x)
  dy <- diff(y)
  pl_ml    <- sum(abs(dx))
  pl_ap    <- sum(abs(dy))
  pl_total <- sum(sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2))
  
  tibble(
    PathLength_AP    = pl_ap,
    PathLength_ML    = pl_ml,
    PathLength_Total = pl_total,
    MeanVelocity_AP  = pl_ap / duration_s,
    MeanVelocity_ML  = pl_ml / duration_s
  )
}

compute_ellipse95 <- function(x, y) {
  n <- length(x)
  cov_mat <- stats::cov(cbind(x, y))
  eig <- eigen(cov_mat)
  Fval <- stats::qf(0.95, df1 = 2, df2 = n - 2)
  area <- 2 * pi * Fval * sqrt(eig$values[1] * eig$values[2])
  
  list(area = area, eig = eig, Fval = Fval, center = c(mean(x), mean(y)))
}

ellipse_boundary_df <- function(x, y, n_points = 100) {
  e <- compute_ellipse95(x, y)
  axis_lengths <- sqrt(2 * e$Fval * e$eig$values)
  theta  <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n_points)
  circle <- rbind(cos(theta), sin(theta))
  pts <- e$eig$vectors %*% diag(axis_lengths) %*% circle
  
  tibble(ex = e$center[1] + pts[1, ], ey = e$center[2] + pts[2, ])
}

compute_trial_features <- function(df) {
  n        <- nrow(df)
  duration <- max(df$Time) - min(df$Time)
  path_m   <- compute_path_metrics(df$COPx, df$COPy, duration)
  ellipse  <- compute_ellipse95(df$COPx, df$COPy)
  time_d   <- diff(df$Time)
  
  bind_cols(
    path_m,
    tibble(
      EllipseArea95     = ellipse$area,
      n_samples         = n,
      duration_s        = duration,
      Fz_min            = min(df$Fz),
      Fz_median         = median(df$Fz),
      time_gap_max      = max(time_d),
      time_nonmonotonic = any(time_d <= 0)
    )
  )
}

# Process trial summary
trial_features <- master %>%
  group_by(Trial, Subject, Vision, Surface, Age, AgeGroup, Gender, Height, Weight, BMI) %>%
  group_modify(~ compute_trial_features(.x)) %>%
  ungroup()

# 2. Structural & Signal QA Checks
modal_n     <- as.integer(names(sort(table(trial_features$n_samples), decreasing = TRUE))[1])
expected_dt <- 0.01

trial_features <- trial_features %>%
  mutate(
    flag_sample_count   = abs(n_samples - modal_n) > 10,
    flag_time_gap       = time_gap_max > (expected_dt * 2) | time_nonmonotonic,
    flag_fz_unweighting = Fz_min < (0.7 * Fz_median),

# 1. Feature Extraction & Ellipse Math
def compute_ellipse95(x, y):
    n = len(x)
    cov_mat = np.cov(x, y)
    eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov_mat)
    f_val = f.ppf(0.95, 2, n - 2)
    area = 2 * np.pi * f_val * np.sqrt(np.maximum(0, eigvals[0] * eigvals[1]))
    return area, eigvals, eigvecs, f_val, np.mean(x), np.mean(y)

def ellipse_boundary_df(x, y, n_points=100):
    area, eigvals, eigvecs, f_val, cx, cy = compute_ellipse95(x, y)
    axis_lengths = np.sqrt(2 * f_val * np.maximum(0, eigvals))
    theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n_points)
    circle = np.vstack([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])
    pts = eigvecs @ np.diag(axis_lengths) @ circle
    return pd.DataFrame({'ex': cx + pts[0, :], 'ey': cy + pts[1, :]})

def compute_trial_features(df):
    duration = df["Time"].max() - df["Time"].min()
    dx = np.diff(df["COPx"])
    dy = np.diff(df["COPy"])
    
    pl_ml  = np.sum(np.abs(dx))
    pl_ap  = np.sum(np.abs(dy))
    pl_tot = np.sum(np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2))
    
    area, _, _, _, _, _ = compute_ellipse95(df["COPx"], df["COPy"])
    time_diffs = np.diff(df["Time"])
    
    return pd.Series({
        "PathLength_AP": pl_ap, "PathLength_ML": pl_ml, "PathLength_Total": pl_tot,
        "MeanVelocity_AP": pl_ap / duration, "MeanVelocity_ML": pl_ml / duration,
        "EllipseArea95": area, "n_samples": len(df), "duration_s": duration,
        "Fz_min": df["Fz"].min(), "Fz_median": df["Fz"].median(),
        "time_gap_max": time_diffs.max(), "time_nonmonotonic": (time_diffs <= 0).any()
    })

title: Static Data Visualization
text:
In this section, we walk through the iterative process of building data visualizations. We start with raw observations, layer on aesthetic mappings and summary geometry, aggregate data to account for repeated measures, and conclude with multi-panel publication figures.



We begin by mapping Surface condition to the x-axis and PathLength_Total to the y-axis. This raw point plot reveals the basic distribution of data but suffers from heavy overplotting across conditions.
It is worth noting that plotnine is a package for Python that uses syntax essentially identical to ggplot in R (both plotnine and ggplot are based on Leland Wilkinson’s “Grammar of Graphics” - a layered system to build data visualizations). However, when making this document using Quarto inside of R Studio, I need to call Python functions using reticulate and - for computing reasons I do not full understand - it is difficult to render plotnine objects through reticulate. Thus, for these examples, I am using matplotlib and seaborn to great plots similar to my ggplot visualizations, but for pragmatic users, it is probably more efficient to learn ggplot/plotnine syntax that is portable across languages.
